subject: surgery
title: Fontaine Classification and Critical Limb Ischaemia

steps.tx: The staging system grading peripheral arterial disease from no symptoms to gangrene is the **Fontaine classification**. Stage one has no symptoms, stage two causes claudication, stage three rest pain and stage four tissue loss. It guides urgency and choice of treatment. Rutherford grading splits stage two further by walking distance and treadmill testing, which Fontaine leaves as one broad group.
steps.say: The Fontaine classification stages arterial disease from silent narrowing to gangrene and guides treatment urgency.

vis.alt: Fontaine and Rutherford staging of peripheral arterial disease.
vis.caption: Fontaine staging of leg arterial disease. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Stage two disease limited to walking pain is Fontaine stage **claudication**. Patients remain safe with medical therapy and exercise in most cases. Intervention is reserved for lifestyle limiting symptoms despite best treatment. Claudication distance under 200 metres is stage 2b, while pain beyond 200 metres is stage 2a.
steps.say: Fontaine stage two claudication is managed medically with exercise unless lifestyle remains severely limited.

steps.tx: This leg shows the end stage that Fontaine staging warns about, with a dusky forefoot, a non-healing ulcer and darkened toes. **Critical limb ischaemia** means perfusion can no longer meet resting tissue needs, so pain persists even without walking. Unlike claudication, this picture demands urgent vascular assessment, because delay converts salvageable tissue into irreversible gangrene requiring major amputation.
steps.say: Dusky toes, ulceration and rest pain mark critical limb ischaemia. Unlike claudication, this foot needs urgent vascular assessment to stay salvageable.

vis.alt: Foot and leg with critical limb ischaemia showing rest pain tissue changes and early gangrene
vis.caption: Critical limb ischaemia with rest pain, ulceration and early gangrenous change in the foot. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Rest pain with ulcers or gangrene together define **critical limb ischaemia**. Without restoring blood flow, major amputation commonly follows within a year. It is now also called chronic limb threatening ischaemia in modern terminology. About one in four patients loses the leg within a year without revascularisation, and heart attack kills more of them than gangrene does.
steps.say: Critical limb ischaemia combines rest pain with tissue loss and commonly leads to amputation without flow restoration.

vis.alt: Advanced peripheral arterial disease with critical ischaemia.
vis.caption: Critical limb ischaemia in arterial disease. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Widening a narrowed artery from inside with a balloon is **angioplasty**. A stent may hold the vessel open afterwards. It suits short narrowings and avoids a major operation in frail patients. Balloon treatment works best on narrowings under 10 centimetres, and drug coated balloons lower the chance of the segment closing again.
steps.say: Angioplasty widens narrowed arteries with a balloon and suits short lesions in frail patients.

steps.tx: Bypassing a long blockage with vein or graft is a **surgical bypass**. The patients own vein gives the most durable result for long occlusions. It remains the best option for extensive disease with good targets. A reversed great saphenous vein graft outperforms artificial grafts below the knee, so the vein is mapped by ultrasound before theatre.
steps.say: Surgical bypass with vein gives the most durable result for long arterial blockages.

steps.tx: Choosing between balloon, bypass and amputation needs a **multidisciplinary decision**. Wound extent, infection and patient fitness all weigh in. Preserving a functional foot is the goal whenever realistically possible. The WIfI score grades the wound, ischaemia and foot infection separately and predicts amputation risk better than stage alone.
steps.say: Multidisciplinary teams weigh wound, infection and fitness to preserve a functional foot whenever possible.

steps.tx: Infection in an ischaemic foot changes everything and demands combined **infection control**. Antibiotics, drainage and urgent flow restoration run together. Operating on blood flow alone while pus spreads invites failure. A hot, swollen ischaemic foot with gas in the tissues needs theatre the same day, not a trial of antibiotics alone.
steps.say: Infected ischaemic feet need antibiotics, drainage and flow restoration together, not flow alone.

steps.tx: Measuring toe pressures helps when ankle vessels are calcified and incompressible, called **toe pressure assessment**. Toes have less calcium, so their pressures reflect true foot perfusion better in diabetics. It refines amputation level decisions too. Toe pressure below 30 millimetres of mercury predicts poor healing, while above 55 usually allows a toe amputation to heal.
steps.say: Toe pressures reflect true foot perfusion better when ankle vessels are calcified in diabetics.

steps.tx: After any revascularisation, long term success depends on continued **secondary prevention**. Antiplatelet drugs, statins, diabetes control and smoking cessation protect the whole circulation. Graft surveillance catches narrowings before they thrombose. Dual pathway treatment with low dose rivaroxaban plus aspirin cuts limb events after revascularisation in trial patients who can take it.
steps.say: Secondary prevention with antiplatelets, statins and surveillance protects grafts and the whole circulation.
